subject: Physics
title: Thermodynamics
summary: Zeroth law: two systems in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other — this is what makes temperature meaningful.
First law: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW (heat given = rise in internal energy + work done BY the gas). For an ideal gas U depends only on temperature.
Work done by a gas = area under the P–V curve. Isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric processes each have their own simple formulas.
Second law: heat does not flow by itself from cold to hot, and no cyclic process can turn heat completely into work. Real processes are irreversible.

formulas.name: First law of thermodynamics
formulas.mistake: Sign convention: heat given TO the gas +, work done BY the gas +. Don't mix conventions.

formulas.name: Work done by a gas
formulas.formula: W = ∫ P dV = area under the P–V curve
formulas.when: Any process drawn on a P–V diagram.
formulas.note: In a cycle, work = area enclosed (clockwise on P–V → positive work).

formulas.name: Internal energy of an ideal gas
formulas.formula: ΔU = n Cv ΔT  (for ANY process)
formulas.note: ΔU depends only on ΔT — use nCvΔT even for non-isochoric processes.

formulas.name: Isothermal process (T constant)
formulas.formula: PV = constant;  ΔU = 0;  W = Q = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 2.303 nRT log(V₂/V₁)
formulas.when: Slow processes in contact with a reservoir.

formulas.name: Adiabatic process (Q = 0)
formulas.formula: PVᵞ = constant;  TVᵞ⁻¹ = constant;  W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1) = nR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1)
formulas.note: The adiabatic curve is steeper (slope −γP/V) than the isothermal one (−P/V).

formulas.name: Mayer's relation and γ
formulas.when: Linking the two molar heat capacities.

formulas.name: Values of Cv and γ
formulas.formula: monoatomic: Cv = 3R/2, γ = 5/3;  diatomic (rigid): Cv = 5R/2, γ = 7/5;  polyatomic (non-linear, rigid): Cv = 3R, γ = 4/3

formulas.name: Fraction of heat turned into work (isobaric)
formulas.when: Diatomic gas: 2/7 of the heat becomes work.

formulas.name: Cyclic process
formulas.formula: ΔU = 0 over a cycle ⇒ Q_net = W_net = area of the loop

examples.title: Isothermal expansion
examples.problem: 2 mol of an ideal gas expand isothermally at 300 K to double the volume. Work done (ln 2 = 0.693)?
examples.solution: W = nRT ln 2 = 2 × 8.314 × 300 × 0.693 ≈ 3458 J (= heat absorbed, since ΔU = 0).

examples.title: Adiabatic compression
examples.problem: A monoatomic gas at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its volume. Final temperature?

examples.title: Isobaric heating of a diatomic gas
examples.problem: 2 mol of a diatomic gas are heated by 50 K at constant pressure. Q, W and ΔU?

examples.title: Work at constant pressure
examples.problem: A gas expands from 1 L to 3 L at 10⁵ Pa. Work done?

examples.title: Adiabatic pressure change
examples.problem: A diatomic gas (γ = 1.4) is compressed adiabatically to half its volume. By what factor does the pressure rise?

examples.title: First law in one line
examples.problem: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work. Change in internal energy?

examples.title: Work in a triangular cycle
examples.problem: A gas goes A(P₀, V₀) → B(2P₀, V₀) → C(2P₀, 2V₀) → back to A along a straight line, with P₀ = 10⁵ Pa and V₀ = 1 L. Net work?
examples.solution: Work = area of the triangle = ½ × V₀ × P₀ = ½ × 10⁻³ × 10⁵ = 50 J.

examples.title: γ of a mixture
examples.problem: 1 mol of a monoatomic gas is mixed with 1 mol of a rigid diatomic gas. γ of the mixture?

topics.title: System, surroundings and state
topics.explain: A system is the part we study; everything else is the surroundings. State variables (P, V, T, U) describe equilibrium states. Extensive variables depend on size (V, U, mass); intensive ones don't (P, T, density).

topics.title: Thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law
topics.explain: If A is in equilibrium with C and B is in equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium. A thermometer works because of this law.

topics.title: Heat, work and internal energy
topics.explain: Heat and work are energy in transit and depend on the path. Internal energy is a state function: in an ideal gas it is purely the kinetic energy of molecules and depends only on T.

topics.title: Reading P–V diagrams
topics.explain: Isobaric: horizontal line; isochoric: vertical line; isothermal: hyperbola; adiabatic: steeper curve. Expansion (V increasing) → W positive; compression → W negative.

topics.title: Quasi-static processes
topics.explain: A process done infinitely slowly so the system is always in equilibrium. Only quasi-static processes can be drawn as curves on a P–V diagram and can be reversible.

topics.title: Reversible and irreversible processes
topics.explain: A reversible process can be run backwards so that both system and surroundings return exactly to the start. Friction, free expansion, heat flow across a finite temperature difference and mixing make processes irreversible. All natural processes are irreversible.

topics.title: Second law of thermodynamics
topics.explain: Kelvin–Planck: no process whose only result is converting heat completely into work. Clausius: no process whose only result is transferring heat from a colder to a hotter body. Both statements are equivalent.

topics.title: Syllabus note
topics.explain: The current NTA syllabus lists the zeroth, first and second laws, processes and reversible/irreversible processes. Heat-engine/refrigerator details and the Carnot cycle are not listed separately, so practise the first law and P–V work most.

ratta: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW;  ΔU = nCvΔT always.
Isothermal: W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁);  adiabatic: PVᵞ = const, W = nRΔT/(γ − 1).
Work = area under P–V;  cycle → area enclosed.
